# Diagnosing Engine Stall and Acceleration Issues After Water Ingress on a 2005 Pontiac G6

When water floods the interior of a vehicle, the immediate instinct is often to focus on upholstery and electronics drying out. However, on a 2005 Pontiac G6 with significant water accumulation on floors, seats, and the dashboard, the real danger lies in submerged sensors and compromised electrical connections. The symptoms you describedâstalling immediately upon engaging Drive or touching the brake pedal, combined with delayed acceleration and eventual stallingâare classic indicators of an engine control unit (ECU) receiving invalid data from moisture-damaged inputs.

The fact that the engine turns over and runs fine in Park suggests the fuel injection system is delivering fuel and the ignition system is firing. The primary failure point here is likely the interaction between the throttle position sensor (TPS) or the accelerator pedal position sensor (APP) and the ECU. Modern engines rely on these sensors to modulate idle speed and allow for acceleration. If water has shorted the circuit in the APP or sent a "floor it" signal due to electrical noise, the ECU may hesitate to open the throttle fully, resulting in the sluggish acceleration you experienced between 1st and 2nd gear.

The specific behavior of stalling when applying the brake pedal is critical. While brake application is normal for an idle engine, if the vehicle stalls immediately upon engaging Drive and pressing the brake, it points toward a failure in the torque converter lockup solenoid or, more likely, a safety interlock logic error triggered by erratic sensor readings. The check engine light illuminating after the flood confirms that the ECU has detected a deviation from expected parameters, such as a lean fuel mixture caused by evaporated water condensing on intake components or a rich mixture from flooded oxygen sensors.

The absence of interior lights prior to the incident is also a significant clue. Many vehicles share wiring harnesses between the lighting circuits and the engine bay ground points. If the water bridge created a short in the chassis ground, it could have disrupted the reference voltage for various sensor arrays, not just the dash lights. This explains why the car drove for 20 yards initially; the system may have defaulted to a "limp mode" or fallback strategy using fixed values for sensors that returned erratic data, allowing movement but preventing high-load acceleration.

To resolve this without immediately dismantling the engine bay, you should inspect the wiring harness where it passes through the firewall and near the floor pans. Look for pinched wires or corrosion on connector housings, specifically those leading to the throttle body and oxygen sensors. Disconnecting the battery is a mandatory first step before touching any engine components after water exposure to prevent short circuits. Once reassembled, clearing the fault codes with an OBDII scanner will tell you if the ECU has reset its adaptive learning values. If the car continues to stall or hesitate, mechanical inspection of the throttle body for water residue and cleaning the air intake system is required before attempting further operation.

While there are diagnostic tools and advanced tuning software available that can help bypass certain sensor faults, relying on a flooded vehicle without professional assessment risks permanent damage to the ECU itself. If you require specialized diagnostic equipment or expert advice on handling post-flood automotive electronics, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can sometimes provide context on managing complex technical workflows, though local automotive electrical specialists remain the most direct path for physical repairs.
